claims.text: The dynamic strength and ductility of solidified FeNiCrMn are governed primarily by the stability and evolution of stacking faults and deformation twins.
FeNiCrMn has a characteristically low stacking-fault energy.
Low stacking-fault energy promotes stacking faults and deformation twins in FeNiCrMn.
TWIP is activated in FeNiCrMn at intermediate and high strain rates and at lower temperatures.
TWIP activation maintains the strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation slip dominates deformation of FeNiCrMn at higher temperatures and lower strain rates.
The target initial state is equiatomic or near-equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn with a single-phase FCC microstructure and minimal pre-existing defects.
Temperature and strain rate modulate the formation of stacking faults and deformation twins through their relationship with stacking-fault energy.
Deformation twins and stacking faults formed under dynamic loading enhance work hardening and ductility through the TWIP effect.
Increasing temperature or decreasing strain rate reduces twinning activity in FeNiCrMn.
Reduced twinning activity can lower work hardening and ductility.
FeNiCrMn will show greater work hardening and ductility at lower temperatures and higher strain rates because twinning is enhanced.
The strength and ductility of FeNiCrMn will decrease at higher temperatures and lower strain rates as twinning diminishes.
The strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn will be comparable to that of CoCrFeMnNi under similar conditions.
CoCrFeMnNi exhibits TWIP behavior because of low stacking-fault energy.
The proposed mechanism is limited to solidified, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn with minimal pre-existing defects under uniaxial loading.
The proposed mechanism is not asserted for substantially compositionally deviated, multiphase, or heavily cold-worked FeNiCrMn.
Direct evidence identifying the dominant dynamic deformation mechanism in FeNiCrMn is limited.
The stacking-fault energy and twinning propensity of FeNiCrMn may differ from those of CoCrFeMnNi.
Failure to observe increased twin and stacking-fault density at lower temperatures and higher strain rates would falsify the proposed mechanism.
